_about: A hand-picked reading list, keyed press:isbn. Nothing computes this — it is a judgement about which forthcoming titles look like a good time, made by reading the jacket copy for the whole season. Edit freely; build.py just merges it in.
chicago:9780226844190: The alligator as a way into how Americans have tried to master, sell, wrestle and finally meme the natural world. Any book whose subtitle travels from first contact to Florida Man knows exactly what it is doing, and 456 pages says the author had a lot of material.
mit:9780262054546: In 1872 a horse flu stopped American cities dead — no deliveries, no fire engines, no streetcars — because the whole economy ran on horses. A genuinely strange pivot point, and the kind of history that quietly rearranges how you see infrastructure.
princeton:9780691239354: Animals self-medicate: ants dose their colonies, chimps eat particular leaves when sick. Eight blurbs on a 272-page trade book from Princeton means they think this one travels, and the premise is irresistible.
yale:9780300282597: A history of smell — the sense with almost no vocabulary and enormous emotional reach. Short, and the kind of subject that makes you notice things for a week afterwards.
mit:9781917674157: James Tilly Matthews believed a machine called the Air Loom was tormenting him from a London cellar in 1796 — the first fully documented case of paranoid delusion, and one that arrived with the machine age. Mike Jay is very good on this territory.
yale:9780300278880: Jay's other book this season, on everyone who has wanted to wire a machine into a brain — visionaries, quacks and surgeons alike. Reading it beside The Influencing Machine gives you two centuries of the same anxiety from both ends.
chicago:9780226851648: Hop-picking was young women's work, and American brewing was built on it. A small, specific, well-blurbed social history of an industry everyone thinks they already know.
princeton:9780691291666: Lilith, traced from Mesopotamian demoness to the template for how the West talks about difficult women. Ambitious and legibly angry, which usually makes for good reading.
princeton:9780691243504: Between 1933 and 1939 Charlotte Beradt secretly collected Germans' dreams as the Reich took hold — people dreaming their own compliance before they could say it awake. Ten blurbs, 152 pages, and unlike anything else on this list.
chicago:9780226851907: Why the search for chemically induced transcendence keeps outliving the religions it was meant to replace. A cultural history rather than a trip report, which is the rarer thing.
harvard:9780674307889: Malcolm Gaskill on why people have kept believing in ghosts, witches and mediums — treating the belief seriously rather than explaining it away. He is one of the best narrative historians working on this, and Harvard rarely gathers eight blurbs.
chicago:9780226840925: Twenty-four insects, twenty-four hours, one hour each. A lovely constraint, illustrated, under 200 pages — the sort of book you finish in two sittings and then quote at people.
princeton:9780691237718: Thomas Seeley has spent a career watching honey bees and this is twenty puzzles he and his colleagues actually solved. Nine blurbs. Field biology written by someone who never got bored of it.
chicago:9780226168456: A year of animal mating, month by month. Faintly ridiculous framing, genuinely good natural history, and the calendar structure means you can dip in anywhere.
mit:9780262054584: Tetris escaped a Soviet research lab and became the best-selling game on earth, via a licensing fight of real legal absurdity. A Cold War story told through a puzzle game.
mit:9780262054911: An unapologetic book about why the brick is fun. Not every pick has to be improving, and MIT lining up four endorsements for a gift book suggests it is better than it needs to be.
princeton:9780691294094: Why the software running everything is so strange, by someone who studies how it breaks. If you have ever wondered whether the weirdness is you or the machine, this is the answer.
chicago:9780226835068: One block in Rome, two thousand years, dug down through the layers. The tight frame is what makes it — city history usually fails by being too big.
princeton:9780691263441: 1688 recast as what it physically was: a Dutch invasion fleet four times the size of the Spanish Armada landing in England. The kind of reframing that makes a familiar story feel new.
princeton:9780691268910: A single medieval rape case followed through the records, and what it does to modern assumptions about what women could expect from law in the 1300s. Narrative history built on one life.
yale:9780300303735: Damrosch on Stevenson, who lived a life at least as adventurous as anything he wrote. Long, but a biographer this good earns 584 pages.
yale:9780300270723: Edith Hall is the most readable classicist in Britain, and Medea is the myth most in need of someone unsentimental. Short and likely sharp.
yale:9780300297164: Medieval magic through twenty manuscripts you can look at — actual grimoires and charm books rather than a survey. Ten blurbs, and Yale illustrate this sort of thing properly.
yale:9780300282511: Tea leaves, tarot, entrails, palms — a global visual history of how people have tried to read the future. Owen Davies writes about the occult without either debunking or swooning.
yale:9780300305326: Constellation myths from cultures that never spoke to each other, including an emu egg hunt in the southern sky. 208 pages, and it will change what you see on a clear night.
chicago:9780226843063: Philip Ball on Niels Bohr, who broke reality more thoroughly than Einstein and is much less well served by biography. Ball is reliably excellent on physics for people who are not physicists.
harvard:9780674300354: One bomb — its ore, its test, its fallout, its politics — followed all the way through. Jon Else is a documentary film-maker, which shows in the structure, and seven blurbs is a lot for Harvard.
mit:9780262052719: A comic demolition of longevity science, including the finding that most of the world's supposed 110-year-olds live in places with bad birth records. Genuinely funny about a field that badly needs it.
mit:9780262054058: Sleep paralysis — the waking terror with a demon sitting on your chest — used as a window into how the brain builds reality. A Harvard sleep researcher writing about the thing itself.
chicago:9780226841021: Walter Jenkins, LBJ's closest aide, arrested in a YMCA men's room weeks before the 1964 election. A small scandal that dragged queer life into national politics, told properly.
yale:9780300267136: Seventeenth-century Nagasaki, where the line between samurai, pirate and merchant was a matter of who was asking. Short, and an unfamiliar corner of a familiar century.
chicago:9780226851976: What is under Sydney Harbour, and what the wrecks and dumped objects say about the city above. Underwater history is a genuinely novel vantage point.
mit:9780262049474: The women who did the computing at the NSA, written by one of them. Codebreaking history usually stops at Bletchley; this carries it into the Cold War.
princeton:9780691293714: Lepore on the stories America tells about its own beginning, and why they keep being rewritten. Essays rather than a doorstop, which suits her.
mit:9781965874240: The Kuchar brothers made gleeful underground trash cinema for fifty years, and this is their memoir. Not respectable, not trying to be.
yale:9780300303797: Dawkins on forty-two of the strangest organisms alive, illustrated. No blurbs yet because it is Yale's lead natural history title and the copy is barely up — worth watching for that reason alone.
chicago:9780226850887: A 1940s cowboy suit that caught fire, the lawsuit that followed, and what the surviving documents do and do not preserve of a life. 672 pages on one accident, which is either indulgent or remarkable.
yale:9780300282337: The carol as a strange survival — pagan, banned, revived, commercialised. Seasonal in the best way, and John Potter is a singer as well as a scholar.
